lines: Notice that this write was never treated carelessly. It followed every rule it was given.
Both replicas the system cared about had it before anyone was told it succeeded.
The problem isn't the rule. It's that the replica which survives is the one the rule never counted.
Before choosing, separate the two switches at play here instead of treating this as one big unknown.
One switch decides how strong the starting promise was. The other decides what happens once that promise is tested by a failure.
Only one of the two actually determines whether the data comes back.
answer: Unclean election is the one that matters here.
Turn it off, and the cluster refuses to move on without a replica that actually has the write — the data is safe, just temporarily out of reach.
Turn it on, and the surviving replica gets to lead anyway, missing write and all. The acknowledgment you were given is suddenly worth nothing.

lines: Watch what's actually guaranteed here versus what's merely likely.
Writes agree with each other and happen in the order a client sent them. That's the whole promise.
A read, though, is handed to you by whichever replica you happen to be talking to — and that replica might not have heard the news yet.
Pay attention to what's being offered as a choice, not a default.
The strong answer is always available. The weaker, faster one is something you have to ask for explicitly, trading freshness for speed on your own terms.
Nobody gets the fast answer by accident here.
Sit with how unusual it is for a system to retire its own foundation after a decade of relying on it.
Years of leaning on one coordination service, and then a release that simply doesn't need it anymore.
What replaced it isn't new. It's the exact mechanism this chapter already opened up.
Notice what's being traded here, because it isn't obvious from the replica count alone.
Needing fewer copies to tolerate the same number of failures sounds like a pure win. It isn't pure.
Every one of those copies now has to show up before anything is called done, which means the slowest one sets the pace, not the fastest.
Separate the protection this setting offers from the protection it still doesn't.
Insisting on every in-sync copy guards against any single one of them disappearing. Letting one copy alone count removes that guard before anything even goes wrong.
And even with the strongest setting, one particular edge case, a last surviving copy corrupting itself on its own restart, still slips through, which is exactly why a dedicated fix exists for it.
Watch what happens to the loser here, because it isn't failure in any ordinary sense.
Two parties building on the same starting point, only one gets to land. The other doesn't error out.
It just looks at what actually won, builds again from there, and tries once more.
Carry forward what's actually shared across every mechanism in this topic, not the four different product names.
A small group of replicas, agreeing on one value, changing that value atomically whenever it needs to change.
Everything else, the session, the quorum shape, the pointer swap, is just which group was handed that one job.
Before answering, think about what that overlapping replica is actually guaranteed to do, not just guaranteed to exist.
Knowing a shared replica is somewhere in the crowd is one fact. Knowing the protocol reliably picks out whatever that replica is holding is a completely different fact.
answer: No, the overlap alone isn't enough.
It guarantees a replica holding the latest write is somewhere inside the overlap, but not that any particular read protocol will notice it and prefer it over everything else it hears back.
You still need a rule, usually versioning or timestamps, for picking the right answer out of that overlap. The overlap just makes picking it possible.
